analysis.one_liner: Restores the top two income tax rates and taxes dividends like ordinary income to pay for Iraq war costs.
analysis.headline: The bill to pay for Iraq war spending by raising taxes on the wealthiest households was sent to two House committees the day it was introduced and never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have paid for $86.6 billion in Iraq and Afghanistan war operations and reconstruction by raising money now instead of borrowing it. It would restore the top two income tax rates to 36% and 39.6%, undoing part of the 2001 tax cuts, and repeal the 2003 cut that taxes stock dividends at the lower capital gains rate. The added revenue would fund military operations and relief and reconstruction in Iraq and Afghanistan for fiscal year 2004.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers generally, and future taxpayers in particular, because the cost of the war would be covered by current tax revenue instead of added to the national debt. Anyone who benefits from a smaller federal deficit, since $86.6 billion in spending would be paid for rather than borrowed.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would appropriate $65.5 billion for military operations in Iraq and in support of the global war on terrorism, and $21.1 billion for relief and reconstruction in Iraq and Afghanistan, for fiscal year 2004.

Instead of borrowing to cover those costs, the bill would raise the revenue first: it restores the top two individual income tax rates to 36% and 39.6% starting in 2004, reversing reductions made by the 2001 tax law.
It repeals the provision of the 2003 tax law that taxed individual dividend income at the lower capital gains rate, so dividends would again be taxed as ordinary income.

The appropriations are designated as emergency requirements under the fiscal year 2004 budget resolution, which allowed the spending outside normal budget limits — paired here with the offsetting revenue.

analysis.who_pays: Households in the top two income tax brackets, who would see their top rates rise from 35% back to 39.6%, and investors who receive stock dividends, who would pay ordinary income rates on that income rather than the 15% capital-gains-rate treatment enacted in 2003. The largest burden would fall on the highest-income taxpayers, who hold most taxable dividends, though middle-income investors with dividend income would pay more too.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the dividend rate cut would raise taxes on dividend income across the income scale, including middle-income and retired investors who live partly off dividends, not only the wealthiest households.

Supporters of keeping the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts argued at the time that lower rates encouraged investment and growth, and that raising them during a slow recovery could weigh on hiring and investment; this is the standard economic objection the bill would have had to answer.

The bill labels the appropriations 'emergency' spending, which sidesteps the budget resolution's normal spending limits — a design choice that weakens budget discipline even in a bill whose stated purpose is fiscal responsibility.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade-off is straightforward: the bill shifts about $86.6 billion of war costs from borrowed money onto taxes paid mostly by high earners and dividend investors, reducing debt for everyone else, at the cost of higher rates for those groups and somewhat higher taxes on dividend income for some middle-income investors. The emergency designation is an honest flaw in a bill named for fiscal responsibility, but it mirrors how the underlying war spending was being handled anyway.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Appropriations Committees the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Wexler introduced the bill on September 9, 2003, as the House was considering the fiscal year 2004 emergency supplemental for Iraq and Afghanistan operations.

The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee (which handles taxes) and the Appropriations Committee (which handles spending), with the Speaker to decide how to split the provisions between them.
No committee action, hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded in the bill's action history after the referral; the last recorded action is the September 9, 2003 referral itself.
The bill had one sponsor and four Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support on record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income taxpayers and dividend investors came out ahead: the top rates and dividend tax treatment of the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts stayed in place, and the war's cost continued to be financed through borrowing rather than a dedicated tax. The outcome also spared members from having to vote on raising taxes during wartime.

for.name: Rep. Robert Wexler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill proposing to pay for the Iraq war supplemental by restoring the top two tax rates and repealing the dividend tax cut.

for.name: 4 House Democrats (cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all four listed cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over the tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 9, 2003 and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or report — so the bill never moved.

against.name: House Appropriations Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over the spending provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 9, 2003 and took no recorded action on the bill.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party leadership controlling the House floor calendar in the 108th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; the majority sets which bills get committee time and votes, and this one received none.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat and no Republican support appears in the record; the bill then died in committee without action under the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill would raise the top two rates back to 39.6% and tax dividends as ordinary income, directly increasing taxes on the wealthiest households, who hold most taxable dividends. Their interest in keeping the lower rates ran against the bill's goal of paying war costs with current revenue.

industries.industry: Defense contractors and military service industries
industries.note: The bill would appropriate $65.5 billion for military operations, money that flows to defense suppliers and support services. Because the bill pays for that spending with taxes rather than borrowing, its gain is tied to a mechanism that costs high earners rather than adding to public debt.
The bill would appropriate $21.1 billion for relief and reconstruction in Iraq and Afghanistan, creating contracts and work for firms in that sector, paid for within the same tax-offset structure.
